data.raw_text:
🚨 The Filipino Communist Party Was at the Battle of Seattle — and ILPS Says Bayan Made It Happen

Bayan and Anakbayan present themselves as legal activist organizations with no formal allegiance to the Communist Party of the Philippines, the underground revolutionary party that has waged a decades-long insurgency through its armed wing, the New People’s Army. Those denials are not optional. They are legally and strategically essential to how both groups operate in the United States and the Philippines.

That is what makes Victor Garcés, a senior leader in the International League of Peoples’ Struggle, so stunningly candid in remarks he delivered last week at ILPS’s 25th anniversary celebration.

Garcés stated outright that Bayan sent a delegation to Seattle in 1999 and brought Jose Maria Sison with them during the WTO protests. Sison was not just any activist. He was the founder and chairman of the Communist Party of the Philippines and the chief ideologue behind the New People’s Army, later designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization by the United States for decades of guerrilla attacks, assassinations, and bombings.

According to Garcés, Sison used that Seattle gathering to call for building a global united front, and attendees moved straight from that forum into the street actions that became the Battle of Seattle. Garcés describes this moment as the spark that pushed Sison to conceptualize what would become the International League of Peoples’ Struggle, now one of the most active global hubs for international anti-imperialist coordination.

The contradiction is unavoidable. Bayan and Anakbayan insist they have no formal ties to the Communist Party of the Philippines, yet their own network brought the party’s chairman to the United States, put him on stage, and folded him directly into one of the most consequential protest moments of the era.

And now, in 2025, ILPS leadership is saying it openly on camera.
